The customer's payment method preference should have been formally escalated and resolved.

column1: Summary: L1 support performed region changes, channel changes, factory reset, manual firmware update, IPv6/DNS/MAC-clone changes, and node isolation testing — all yielding no improvement beyond 500 Mbps wireless — before escalating to CAT, where the case is now pending a callback.

Insights: The factory reset produced a temporary improvement to 800 Mbps that regressed within two days, strongly suggesting a software/firmware regression or a settings-related throughput cap being re-applied after the device re-learns its environment. The gap between wired (900 Mbps) and wireless (500 Mbps) persisting even when standing next to the primary node alone points to a device-specific Wi-Fi radio or firmware limitation rather than a mesh backhaul or placement issue.

column3:
>
  • Missing diagnostic — RF environment and band steering not investigated: Agent changed channels but never verified whether the iPhone 17 Pro Max was actually connecting to the 6 GHz band (MBE7000 is a tri-band Wi-Fi 6E/7 router). If the device was connecting on 5 GHz instead of 6 GHz, this alone would explain the 500 Mbps cap. The agent should have confirmed the connected band and frequency in the router admin panel before attempting any other changes.
  • Missing diagnostic — no check of maximum link/negotiated PHY rate: At no point was the reported link speed (Tx/Rx rate) of the iPhone checked in the router's client list. This is a critical step to distinguish between a Wi-Fi association bottleneck and an actual throughput issue.
  • Incorrect or premature step — changing transmission region to 'United States' for a Hong Kong customer: Setting the wireless region to the US on a device used in Hong Kong is both technically incorrect and potentially a regulatory violation. The correct region should be Hong Kong or China. This could also affect allowable channels and power levels, potentially degrading performance.
  • No baseline speed test methodology established: All speed tests were done using a single app (implied) on iPhone. The agent never instructed the customer to test on a laptop via Wi-Fi or use a consistent speed test server, making comparisons unreliable. A controlled test (same device, same server, same location, same time of day) was never performed.
  • DNS change to 114.114.114.114 / 8.8.8.8 is irrelevant to wireless throughput: Changing DNS servers does not affect raw Wi-Fi data transfer speed in a speed test. This step added noise to the troubleshooting without diagnostic value and should not have been applied as a throughput fix.
  • MAC address cloning (address cloning) disabled without documented rationale: Disabling MAC cloning is an ISP-facing WAN setting and has no effect on local wireless LAN speeds. This step was irrelevant to the reported problem and indicates the agent was applying a generic checklist rather than targeted diagnostics.
  • 5-day gap before escalation write-up was submitted (ticket created 2026-05-14, escalation email sent 2026-05-21): The customer had already called back multiple times during this period. The escalation should have been initiated much sooner given that the initial L1 steps failed and the customer was repeatedly calling.
  • CAT agent (eric.marbella) delayed actioning the ticket due to being on another call, and explicitly noted this in the ticket: While understandable, this resulted in the ticket sitting unactioned for several hours after being claimed. The agent should have either not claimed the ticket until available, or arranged for another CAT agent to cover it promptly.
  • No factory reset with firmware downgrade or alternate firmware tested: Given that the reset temporarily restored 800 Mbps and the speed regressed within two days, no attempt was made to test whether the current firmware version (1.0.14.216607) is the cause of the regression. A factory reset followed by NOT restoring settings, or testing a prior firmware, was never attempted.
  • No question asked about what changed between the reset and the regression: The agent did not ask the customer what settings or devices were reconnected after the reset that might have triggered the speed drop back to 500 Mbps — this could have identified the exact configuration causing the issue.

This was incorrect — the agent should have reviewed the prior ticket, identified what was already tried, and avoided repeating steps already completed (e.g. DNS settings were already confirmed consistent with prior troubleshooting, making the DNS review redundant from the start).
  • Wrong factory reset instruction: The agent instructed the customer to hold the reset button until the red light 'completely goes out.' The correct MX4200 factory reset procedure requires holding the button until the light turns RED and then releasing — not waiting for it to extinguish. Releasing at the wrong time risks an incomplete reset, which undermines the entire troubleshooting step.
  • Premature escalation path chosen incorrectly: After all troubleshooting was exhausted and the device is still under warranty, the agent should have proactively offered an RMA/replacement rather than informing the customer the ticket would be escalated to the CAT team. The customer had to demand a replacement instead of being offered one — this is a service failure.
  • Unnecessary troubleshooting burden on customer: Given this is a known recurring issue unresolved since at least February of the prior year and the device is under active warranty, the extensive multi-step troubleshooting session (firmware update, reset, IPv6, MAC cloning, static DNS) should not have been required of the customer at all. The correct approach after identifying this as a repeat unresolved issue would have been to fast-track to replacement.
  • CMD screenshot request was unnecessary and friction-causing: Asking the customer for a CMD screenshot after already performing extensive troubleshooting steps with no resolution added no diagnostic value and directly contributed to customer dissatisfaction and the complaint. This step should have been skipped in favor of proceeding to replacement.
  • Agent suggested secondary router (double-NAT) workaround inappropriately: The agent proposed a 'secondary router solution' as a potential fix. This is not an appropriate troubleshooting or resolution step for a device under warranty with a suspected hardware defect — it is a workaround that would degrade network performance and does not resolve the root issue. The customer correctly refused.
  • Email-first response asked only for a diagnostics log before any triage: The initial email response skipped all basic triage questions (symptoms, frequency, setup details) and jumped directly to requesting a diagnostic report, then promised escalation to senior engineers. This created an expectation mismatch since the next contact was a standard troubleshooting call, not a senior engineer review.
  • Callback and resolution timeline too long: Informing the customer to expect a response by Tuesday or Wednesday the following week (approximately 5–7 days) for a P2 warranted, repeat-contact issue with a CSAT of 1 is unacceptable. The replacement decision should have been made same-day given the circumstances.
  • No proactive acknowledgment of prior unresolved contact: Neither the email nor the phone call included an apology or acknowledgment that the issue was reported and unresolved previously, which contributed to the customer's complaint about Linksys's support process.

column1: Insights: Multiple troubleshooting steps were performed in a single call without first establishing whether the problem was reproducible at that moment, suggesting a reactive rather than diagnostic approach. The customer has now contacted support at least twice without resolution, leading to deep frustration and a replacement demand — the repeated failure to resolve a known recurring issue is a clear pattern indicating this likely requires hardware replacement or deeper ISP-level investigation.

column4:
it should not have been offered at this stage.
  • The agent performed multiple sequential configuration changes (firmware update, factory reset, IPv6 disable, MAC clone, static DNS) all in one call without isolating variables between steps. This makes it impossible to determine which change, if any, had an effect and is poor diagnostic methodology. Each change should be tested in isolation.
  • Factory reset instructions were incorrect or poorly described: the agent told the customer to hold reset until the red light 'completely goes out,' but the MX4200 reset procedure requires releasing when the light changes to indicate reset mode — the customer then reported a solid purple light, suggesting possible confusion or incorrect reset guidance.
  • The agent asked the customer to provide CMD screenshot results after already performing a factory reset and reconfiguration — this is a missed diagnostic step that should have been performed before making any changes, to capture the baseline network state.
  • The first support contact in February of the prior year (referenced by both the customer and internal notes) did not resolve the issue. There is no evidence that the agent reviewed the prior case history or its findings before starting a new troubleshooting sequence, resulting in duplicated effort and customer frustration.
  • The initial email response from support only asked for a diagnostic log and immediately mentioned escalation, without asking basic qualifying questions (e.g. when did the issue start again, was the device in storage, what changed). This is a missed triage opportunity.
  • The agent suggested the CAT team escalation path to the customer, but the customer refused. At this point, given the device is under warranty, has a known recurring unresolved issue, and the customer is uncooperative with further diagnostics, the appropriate next step should have been to proactively offer a warranty replacement rather than continuing to push diagnostics — escalating internally without communicating a clear resolution path to the customer caused further frustration.
  • The callback was scheduled vaguely for '3:30 PM' without confirming timezone or date with the customer, and the expected resolution window of 'Tuesday or Wednesday next week' was communicated without a firm commitment or case reference, which is unprofessional and adds to customer dissatisfaction.
  • No attempt was made to check with the ISP (Netvigator) whether there are known outages or account-level issues — given wired connections also drop intermittently, an ISP-side issue cannot be ruled out and should have been investigated or at least suggested.

column1: Insights: The core troubleshooting was methodical but took far too long to isolate that both devices may be faulty — MBE7000's disconnection was only surfaced on 26 May. The RMA approval decision on 14 April was correct but was immediately stalled by requesting documents the customer had partially already submitted, and no one acknowledged or actioned the diagnostic report the customer sent in March, which is a significant internal communication failure.

>
  • MISSED ESCALATION TRIGGER: The first L1 agent marked the ticket as 'Resolved' immediately on first contact (10 Mar) even though no troubleshooting was completed and the call dropped. This was incorrect — the status should never have been set to Resolved without confirmed resolution.
  • REPEATED QUESTION ALREADY ANSWERED: On 15 May, Xiaoge Ji emailed customer requesting the backend diagnostic report screenshot. The customer had already submitted this on 18 March. No agent had read or actioned the March submission. This is an internal failure that severely damaged customer trust and wasted 2 months.
  • MISSING SYSINFO COLLECTION: HQ (John Pagurayan) issued clear diagnostic instructions on 18 March — sysinfo capture, ping test, standalone LN1400 test with Wi-Fi disabled. These steps were never confirmed as completed across the entire case. Agents should have executed and documented these before any further escalation or RMA discussion.
  • DELAYED RMA DECISION: Despite Kris Qin approving the refund/replacement on 14 April, no RMA was initiated until document collection was requested again — and even then the process stalled. Given the warranty was active and multiple TS steps had been exhausted since March, the RMA decision should have come weeks earlier.
  • NO ACKNOWLEDGEMENT OF CUSTOMER'S ESCALATING FRUSTRATION: Customer sent replacement/timeline demand emails on 18 Mar, 28 Apr, and 5 May with no substantive response. Each unanswered email increased dissatisfaction. A dedicated response with a timeline should have been sent after the first unanswered escalation email.
  • INCOMPLETE DIAGNOSTIC ON MBE7000: Throughout the case the MBE7000 was assumed to be working correctly when used as the parent node. It was only on 26 May that MBE7000 was confirmed to also disconnect. Agents should have proactively tested MBE7000 in isolation far earlier (by mid-March at latest) to determine if the problem was device-specific or environmental/ISP-related.
  • WRONG CHANNEL SELECTION ADVICE: On 11 Mar, the agent instructed the customer to set the 6GHz channel to '5.92'. This is not a valid standard Wi-Fi channel number for 6GHz (valid channels are 1–233 in steps of 4, e.g. 1, 5, 9 etc., or by centre frequency in GHz such as 5.945 GHz). This was incorrect advice and should have been verified before instructing the customer.
  • UNNECESSARY NODE ROLE REVERSAL WITHOUT ISP ISOLATION: Before swapping parent/child node roles, agents should have first isolated whether the issue was ISP/modem-related by connecting a single device directly to the modem. No ISP-side diagnostic was ever performed despite HKBN being identified as the ISP.
  • INTERNAL HANDOFF FAILURES: Multiple agents handled this case (Xiaoge Ji, Zhiliang Chen, Weiyu Zeng, Xiangjie Zhang, Kris Qin, John Pagurayan, Jane Reambonanza) with poor documentation continuity — evidenced by the repeated requests for already-submitted documents and the 19-day gap (25 Mar to 13 Apr) with no action.
  • NO TIMELINE OR SLA COMMITMENT GIVEN TO CUSTOMER: Despite multiple explicit requests for a written timeline, no agent ever provided one. This is a basic customer service obligation that was ignored throughout the case.
  • CONSUMER COUNCIL THREAT NOT FORMALLY FLAGGED IN TICKET: The customer's threat to escalate to the Consumer Council (26 May) was mentioned in a note by Kris Qin but was not formally flagged with a priority escalation or management notification in the ticket system. This requires immediate management attention.

column3:
>
  • Requesting a diagnostics log as the very first response — before any basic triage questions — was premature and contributed directly to the CSAT score of 1. The agent should have first acknowledged the issue, asked basic qualifying questions (firmware version, when issue occurs, wired vs wireless, etc.) and attempted guided troubleshooting before requesting a log upload.
  • The ticket was marked 'Resolved' at creation (07:59:52) before any contact or resolution occurred. This is a workflow/status integrity violation and likely inflated resolution metrics incorrectly.
  • The agent suggested a 'secondary router (double NAT)' workaround as an early option. This is inappropriate advice for a single-node mesh product experiencing intermittent connectivity — it addresses symptoms of a different problem and was rightly rejected by the customer. It should not have been proposed.
  • The prior unresolved contact from February 2025 was acknowledged but not properly leveraged — the agent stated previous diagnostics were no longer relevant and restarted from scratch. The prior case notes and troubleshooting outcomes should have been reviewed to avoid repeating failed steps and to target remaining unexplored causes.
  • The agent was unable to obtain a CMD screenshot from the customer, yet the escalation notes do not document what specific CMD output was needed or why, nor was an alternative method offered (e.g., Linksys app diagnostics, ping test via router admin UI). This is a missed diagnostic opportunity.
  • There was a 4-day gap (22 May to 26 May) with no visible action or update to the customer after the escalation was raised. The customer was told to expect a reply by Tuesday/Wednesday the following week but no outbound contact or update is recorded. This represents a potential callback/follow-up breach.
  • Ashley Alayon's response on 26 May — that further troubleshooting is required before replacement — was correct in policy but provided no actionable next steps, specific tests to run, or escalation path (e.g., CAT L2 involvement). The guidance was insufficient to move the case forward.
  • Kris Qin's escalation message to Ashley Alayon on 22 May was sent but not responded to for 4 days. A follow-up was needed sooner, and the internal SLA for escalation responses should have been enforced. The customer was left without progress during this period.
  • The customer explicitly stated they have had this issue since at least February 2025 and switched to another brand's router because the MX4200 was never fixed. This long-standing fault pattern and customer sentiment were not adequately factored into the replacement decision discussion — a goodwill exception or expedited hardware verification process should have been considered given the warranty is active.
  • The email response from the agent was signed as 'Kelly Cheung' in the quoted footer, yet the ticket is assigned to Xiangjie Zhang. This identity mismatch in agent signatures could cause customer confusion and is a quality/professionalism issue.

column1: Summary: Over 11 weeks, agents attempted warranty documentation collection, internal RMA approval, multiple failed callback attempts, referral to Synnex (which failed due to chatbot-only responses), and then redirection to ISP CSL — none of which have yet resolved the customer's hardware replacement.

Insights: The case has stalled in a loop of handoffs — first to Synnex, then to CSL — without any party taking direct ownership of the replacement. Each redirection increases customer frustration and the risk of public escalation, and as of the last update (26 May) the customer has still not contacted the correct CSL number provided.

column3:
>
  • MISSED DIAGNOSTIC STEP ON INITIAL CALL: The L1 agent only attempted one troubleshooting step (20-second reset) before immediately moving to warranty claim. Standard protocol should include verifying power supply, checking for LED sequence, and attempting a different power source before declaring the device faulty.
  • DOCUMENTATION REQUEST MISMATCH: Kris instructed the agent to request a video, but the earlier email to the customer asked only for receipt, SN photo, and power adapter photo. These two documentation requests were inconsistent and sent separately, causing confusion. A single, comprehensive documentation checklist should have been sent in one message.
  • GOOGLE DRIVE LINK NOT ACCESSIBLE — 16 MAR TO 18 MAR DELAY: The agent did not flag the broken link until 18 March (2 days later), despite noticing 44 minutes were spent on the ticket on 18 March with no action note. The link issue should have been flagged immediately upon receipt.
  • UNEXPLAINED ~2-WEEK GAP (18 MAR TO 03 APR): There is a 16-day gap between the last customer follow-up (18 Mar) and the next internal note (03 Apr). No follow-up was sent to the customer during this period. This is a major SLA and engagement failure.
  • TANGO CARD REFUND OFFERED WITHOUT APPARENT POLICY CHECK: The thread implies a Tango Card refund was proposed to the customer before the RMA/replacement route was fully exhausted. Offering a gift card to a customer whose device is in-warranty and eligible for a physical replacement is incorrect sequencing and likely a policy misstep.
  • ASHLEY ALAYON'S INSTRUCTIONS ARRIVED ON 07 MAY — 34 DAYS AFTER ESCALATION ON 03 APR: The escalation to Ashley was raised on 03 April
column4:
her first substantive instructions were not given until 07 May — a 34-day internal response gap. This is an unacceptable management delay on a P2 ticket with escalation threats.
  • CALLBACK PROMISED FOR 08 MAY AT 13:00 BUT CALLS MADE TO WRONG NUMBER: Kris confirmed the callback would be to +85291447149, but the customer had clarified she would be away from that phone. Agents should have confirmed the alternate number (98249819) before the scheduled call, not after the customer complained. The promise of 13:00 was also not met precisely.
  • CUSTOMER ACCUSED AGENTS OF LYING ('又講大話'): This is a trust-breaking moment that should have triggered immediate supervisor intervention or a direct manager callback — instead it was handled with a text explanation only.
  • SYNNEX REFERRAL MADE WITHOUT VERIFYING SYNNEX CONTACT WAS FUNCTIONAL: Agents directed the customer to Synnex WhatsApp before confirming that real agents (not chatbots) were available on that channel. This was verified only after the customer reported the issue. Agents should pre-test or confirm channel availability with the distributor before referring customers.
  • CSL REFERRAL CONTRADICTS RMA APPROVAL ALREADY IN PLACE: An RMA to Synnex was already approved (custom fields confirm RMA approved by Ivan Chen). Redirecting the customer to contact her ISP (CSL) for a Linksys hardware RMA is incorrect and inconsistent with the approved RMA path. This appears to be advice from the Sales team (via Davis) that contradicts the existing RMA approval.
  • KRIS'S CONCERN ABOUT CSL REDIRECT WAS VALID BUT OVERRULED WITHOUT RESOLUTION: Kris correctly flagged on 14 May that asking the customer to call CSL again would appear as responsibility-dodging. Ashley's response was simply to forward the Sales team instruction without addressing Kris's concern or providing a better solution.
  • CUSTOMER PRIVACY CONCERN NOT FORMALLY ACKNOWLEDGED: When the customer raised concern about 1010 promoting packages and potential data leakage, no formal acknowledgment or data privacy assurance was provided. This should have been addressed explicitly.
  • CASE STILL OPEN AND UNRESOLVED AFTER 11 WEEKS ON A P2 TICKET: As of 26 May, the customer has not completed any RMA step and has a follow-up scheduled for 29 May. The ticket remains in 'New' status with no resolution in sight despite an approved RMA.
  • TICKET STATUS MANAGEMENT POOR: The ticket was briefly set to 'Pending' then reverted to 'New' on 08 May with no clear rationale. Ticket status does not accurately reflect case progression throughout the thread.

column1: The case was resolved in under 4 minutes with no confirmed fix — the node issue was not verified as resolved before closure. The customer did not have physical access to the devices, which severely limited effective troubleshooting, yet the ticket was closed anyway.

🎯 Opportunities
  • Ticket closed without confirmed resolution — the agent closed the case as 'Resolved' despite the customer not having physical access to the nodes and no successful fix being confirmed. The ticket should have been left open or a follow-up scheduled.
  • No model number or serial number collected — the agent noted the customer did not know the model, but no attempt was made to help identify it (e.g., via the Linksys app, router admin page, or purchase receipt). This is a missed diagnostic step.
  • No account or device verification performed — there is no indication the agent checked the customer's Linksys app account, node status, or any cloud-based diagnostics to assess the offline node remotely.
  • Firmware reflash mentioned without context — the agent warned the customer not to perform a reflash alone, but it is unclear why reflashing was being discussed for a single offline node. This may have been premature or irrelevant advice that could confuse the customer.
  • Five-press procedure explained without confirming model compatibility — the five-press reset is model-specific. Since the model was unknown, advising this procedure without first identifying the device was potentially incorrect guidance.
  • No follow-up or callback scheduled — the agent simply told the customer to 'call us back,' placing the burden entirely on the customer. A proactive follow-up or scheduled callback should have been offered given the unresolved nature of the issue.
  • Ticket categorised as 'Presales Inquiry' in custom fields — this is clearly a technical support/connectivity issue, not a presales inquiry. Miscategorisation affects reporting accuracy and routing.

✅ Recommended Next Steps
  • Reopen ticket and schedule a follow-up call once the customer has physical access to the nodes
  • Identify node model and serial number via the Linksys app or label on the device
  • Use remote/cloud diagnostics in the Linksys app to assess the offline node status
  • Correct the ticket category from 'Presales Inquiry' to 'Technical Support / Connectivity'

column1: The support team collected substantial diagnostic evidence early (Linux kernel logs, custom daemon reports, sysinfo logs, beta firmware trial) that strongly indicated a hardware or persistent firmware defect on the child node, yet continued requesting further isolation steps rather than initiating RMA. The pattern of escalating customer frustration, worsening incident frequency, remote-work impact, and a CSAT of 1 all signal that the troubleshooting loop was prolonged well beyond a reasonable threshold for a device under active warranty.

🎯 Opportunities
  • RMA not initiated despite clear hardware evidence: By 22–23 April, Linux kernel logs from three different computers with different Ethernet chipsets unambiguously showed physical carrier loss on the child node's Ethernet port. The customer's explicit RMA request on 23 April and again on 14 May was deflected each time with another diagnostic step. Given the device is in-warranty and the evidence ruled out client-side causes, RMA should have been offered no later than 24 April.
  • Beta firmware deployment was premature and inconclusive: Pushing a beta firmware (1.0.14.216827) without first completing basic isolation (e.g., wired backhaul test) added complexity and false hope. The issue persisted on beta firmware, but the team still did not pivot to RMA.
  • Network topology requested too late and repeatedly: Eric Marbella requested the network topology on 24 April (as an internal note) and again on 14 May. The formal request to the customer was not sent until 14 May — three weeks after it was first identified as needed. This caused unnecessary delay and redundant internal discussion.
  • Wired backhaul isolation test requested too late and context was wrong: The isolation test (connecting child directly to parent via Ethernet) was first mentioned on 13 May — nearly four weeks into the case. Moreover, the customer had already demonstrated the fault occurs on the child node regardless of wireless backhaul conditions
column2:
this test added no new diagnostic value at that stage and the customer correctly challenged its purpose.
  • Customer's explicit RMA request on 14 May was not acknowledged or escalated: When the customer stated 'why not apply the warranty and send the nodes to you so your engineers can do all the tests,' this was a clear escalation trigger and RMA request. Bless responded by asking for network topology again. This was a direct policy failure — customer warranty rights were not actioned.
  • Ticket auto-resolved while issue was unresolved: The ticket was set to Pending on 26 May and auto-resolved on 28 May with no follow-up attempt to the customer. Auto-resolve should not be applied to open hardware fault cases with a documented DSAT risk and no confirmed resolution.
  • Callback promise on 18 April was not followed through on the Monday: Eric Marbella promised contact 'during business hours starting Monday' (21 April). The record shows Bless made a call on 21 April, but no confirmation that this was within the promised Monday window or that the customer was actually reached — the call log just shows a dial attempt and log collection. This should be confirmed as a kept or missed commitment.
  • Missed clarification on node reboot vs. carrier drop: When the customer flagged that the sysinfo endpoint was unreachable during incidents and suggested both nodes rebooted, the team did not investigate or respond to this important finding. A node reboot during a carrier-drop event is a distinct and serious symptom that should have been escalated to engineering immediately.
  • Sysinfo Analyzer tool compatibility issue raised too late: Eric Marbella noted on 15 May that PDF format is incompatible with Sysinfo Analyzer v7 and instructed .txt format. This should have been specified in the very first log collection request on 21 April, avoiding weeks of potentially unusable log files.
  • No proactive update to customer between 29 April and 5 May (6 days silence): The customer had to follow up himself. For a P2 case involving a remote worker experiencing daily outages, a maximum 24–48 hour update cycle should have been maintained.
  • DSAT score of 1 with FCR of 4+ contacts: This case had at minimum four prior contacts before the current ticket. The failure to resolve a straightforward in-warranty hardware fault across multiple contacts over more than a month represents a systemic case-handling failure, not just an individual agent issue.

column1: The case deteriorated significantly after the initial RMA approval due to poor internal handoff, a critical 2.5-month silence after the customer submitted bank details, and an unexplained and unjustified reduction of the agreed refund amount. The repeated changes to refund method and amount without clear policy justification caused serious customer dissatisfaction and a formal complaint.

🎯 Opportunities
  • Agent Xiaoge Ji asked for the purchase invoice on 17 Dec after it had already been implicitly included with the customer's initial submission — this was a redundant request that added friction early in the process.
  • Ticket was incorrectly resolved by Ivan Chen on 17 Dec and again by Xiaoge Ji on 06 Jan before the customer had confirmed acceptance of the refund offer — closing tickets prematurely is a process violation that masked the open action item.
  • After customer submitted bank details on 17 Mar 2026, there was zero follow-up for approximately 2.5 months until the customer chased on 14 Apr 2026. This is a critical SLA breach and the single biggest failure in the case.
  • Xiaoge Ji changed the refund amount from the agreed HKD 1,789.92 to HKD 888.99 on 14 Apr 2026 without any explanation of why the formula changed, and without management approval noted — this constitutes a unilateral breach of a prior agreement and should have required supervisor sign-off.
  • Changing the payment method from bank transfer (previously agreed) to gift card only, without customer consent, is a policy concern — if gift card is the only method, this should have been communicated at the very first refund offer on 30 Dec, not introduced months later after bank details were already collected.
  • The initial refund formula used on 30 Dec (2880 x 0.05% x 757 days) and the revised formula on 14 Apr (2880 x 338/1095) are completely different depreciation methodologies applied to the same case — no justification or internal note was provided for the change. This inconsistency is a major QA failure.
  • On 13 May, Xiaoge Ji offered yet another resolution path (handle via SYNNEX) — this is the third different resolution approach offered, indicating a lack of a clear and consistent refund policy being applied to this case.
  • The original RMA was approved for model FGW5500 but the customer was told by the distributor the out-of-stock model was FGMM1000 — these are different model numbers. No agent clarified or questioned this discrepancy in the thread.
  • The case took approximately 5 months and 11 days from creation (17 Dec 2025) to final resolution (28 May 2026) — entirely unacceptable for a straightforward in-warranty hardware failure with an agreed refund.
  • Xiaoge Ji resolved the ticket on 28 May after advising the customer to contact SYNNEX directly — it is unclear whether the HKD 888.99 cash refund has actually been processed or confirmed by SYNNEX, meaning the case may have been closed without verified resolution.

column1: The troubleshooting path correctly led to an RMA conclusion, but the case is stalled with no resolution path communicated to the customer. The RMA process has hit a dead end with no stock and no escalation to resolve the supply issue, leaving the customer without a working product for over 9 days since ticket creation.

🎯 Opportunities
  • Duplicate email sent: Two identical emails requesting screenshots/videos were sent within 1 minute of each other (02:48:04 and 02:48:51). This is unprofessional and should have been caught before sending.
  • Promised callback not delivered: During the phone call on 03 Jun, the agent promised to call the customer at 10am the next morning. No record of this callback appears in the thread. The customer had to follow up via email themselves.
  • Wrong product name used in email subject: The agent'
column4: in the subject line, while the customer&#x27
column5:
s product is MX6200/MX6201. This creates confusion and suggests insufficient attention to product details.
  • Unnecessary video compression instructions: When the customer said the video was too large to attach, the agent spent time giving multi-step video compression instructions. Given that the customer had already provided a clear written description of the LED behaviour, screenshots would have sufficed. The agent should have accepted the text description and proceeded.
  • Rescue mode procedure may be incorrect: The rescue mode described (power on 30s, power off 30s, repeat three times) does not match the standard MX6200 rescue mode procedure. The correct procedure typically requires holding the reset button during power-on cycles. This should have been verified before advising the customer.
  • Reset troubleshooting performed without WAN cable connected: The customer stated the MX6200 WAN port was not connected to any upstream device during reset attempts. column1: The replacement centre is consistently unreachable by phone across three separate attempts spanning seven days, creating a complete blockage in the RMA process. The agent is recycling apology responses with no escalation to a higher authority or alternative resolution path, leaving an in-warranty customer without any functioning router for over two weeks.

🎯 Opportunities
  • Missed escalation to supervisor/operations manager: After the first unanswered call to the replacement centre on 05 Jun, the agent should have immediately escalated to a Team Coach or Operations Manager to unblock the RMA. Instead, the agent continued sending holding emails for seven more days with no management involvement.
  • No alternative contact method for replacement centre: The agent called only one number three times with no answer. There should be an escalation email, internal ticketing system, or secondary contact for the replacement centre. Relying solely on one unanswered phone number is a process failure.
  • 48-hour SLA was breached without proactive notification: The agent promised a 48-hour response on 04 Jun but had no concrete update until 08 Jun (4 days later) — and only because the customer followed up. The agent should have proactively communicated the delay before the SLA expired.
  • Refund option not proactively offered: By 08 Jun, when it was clear no stock was available and no timeline could be given, the agent should have proactively presented a refund as an alternative. Instead, the customer had to request this themselves on 11 Jun, further delaying resolution.
  • Internal tag to Kris Qin on 05 Jun produced no visible outcome: The agent tagged Kris Qin (apparent CAT L2) in an internal note but there is no follow-up, reply, or action from Kris Qin visible in the thread. This escalation appears to have been ignored and the agent did not follow up on it.
  • Repetitive holding replies with no new information: The agent sent substantially identical apology emails on 08 Jun (twice), 09 Jun, and 11 Jun without any new actionable information. This wastes customer patience and violates basic service standards. Each reply should contain a concrete next step or updated timeline.
  • No case priority upgrade or flagging: This customer has been without a router since 26 May — over two weeks — is borrowing equipment, and has a brand-new in-warranty device. The case should have been flagged as high-urgency/priority escalation well before the customer demanded a refund.
  • Ticket subject says MX6201 but custom fields and customer messages say MX6200: This product model discrepancy was never identified or corrected by the agent, which could cause issues in RMA processing or stock lookup.

column1: The technical diagnosis was handled adequately, but the post-diagnosis warranty resolution path was poorly communicated to the customer — offering only HKD 456 against a HKD 2,000+ device without transparent explanation of the refund calculation methodology created unnecessary escalation. The case closure by Kris Qin with no customer confirmation while the customer is actively disputing the outcome is a significant process failure and KPI manipulation risk.

🎯 Opportunities
  • TECHNICAL — Firmware recovery attempt skipped: Before declaring hardware failure on a boot-loop symptom, agents must attempt a forced recovery (TFTP or recovery mode procedure per FGW5500 service SOP). This was never attempted.
  • TECHNICAL — Power supply not eliminated: Agents did not ask the customer to test with a known-good power adapter before concluding the unit is defective.
  • PROCESS — 6-day internal escalation lag (09 Jun to 15 Jun) with no interim customer update: Customers in active troubleshooting must receive a status update within 1 business day if resolution is pending internal review.
